implementation_notes: Ruby's answer is the block: Thread::Mutex#synchronize locks, runs the block and unlocks in an ensure, so an exception or a non-local exit cannot leak the lock, and Monitor provides the reentrant variant for nested calls. Because the critical section is a block, no explicit unlock exists in ordinary code; bare lock/unlock survives only for condition-variable hand-offs, where ConditionVariable#wait requires the mutex to be held while waiting. The same block shape appears for cross-process coordination (File#flock inside a block), but only database transactions protect data shared between processes.
pitfalls: Mutex#synchronize serializes threads of one process only; multiple workers or processes need database or file locks, so in-process and cross-process policies must be designed together.
Holding the mutex across I/O serializes the application, and a non-reentrant Mutex deadlocks on nested synchronize - use Monitor for reentrancy.
The GVL does not make compound operations atomic: a bare @balance += cents outside synchronize is still racy under threads.

variants.name: Active Record #with_lock and transaction blocks
variants.implementation_notes: Rails makes the offline lock literal: record.with_lock runs the block inside a transaction with the row already locked and saves afterwards, so the database lock's lifetime equals the block's and the framework - not the controller - acquired it; Model.transaction wraps any unit of work the same way, and lock! takes the row lock explicitly when the set of locked rows is decided at runtime. Hand-writing the transaction plus select_for_update pair stays justified when the locked set spans several records or a custom query, since with_lock covers exactly one record.
variants.code_sketch:
account = Account.find(params[:id])
account.with_lock do                    # transaction + row lock, released at block end
  account.balance -= 100
  account.save!                         # no commit or unlock calls in business code
end
pitfalls: with_lock reloads the record and saves it inside the transaction, so changes made to the in-memory object before the call are discarded by the reload.
The row lock lives until the transaction commits: callbacks, external calls or slow work inside the block hold it, and contention shows up as database lock waits, not as Ruby exceptions.
with_lock locks one row; an aggregate modified through several records is not protected as a unit - use a transaction plus explicit locks or a coarse-grained lock.
